stages.theme: The Chess World — rules, pieces, first checkmates, first tactics
primary_concepts: The rook: straight-line movement along files and ranks, and capturing by landing on an enemy piece
The bishop's diagonal movement and its light/dark-square identity
The queen as rook + bishop combined; the most powerful piece
The king moves one square in any direction; the piece you must protect
The knight's L-shaped jump; the only piece that leaps over others
Pawn movement: forward march, two-square first move, diagonal capture
Review of all six pieces' movement and captures
Correct board setup ('light on right', 'queen on her colour')
A pawn reaching the last rank becomes a queen (or other piece)
How captures work; noticing when a piece is attacked
Relative piece values (P1, N3, B3, R5, Q9) and counting material
Introducing THE LOOK: check piece safety before every move
Review of setup, promotion, captures, values, and THE LOOK
Check: attacking the enemy king
The three ways out of check: move, block, capture
Checkmate: a check with no escape — the goal of chess
Distinguishing check, checkmate, and 'not mate' (escape exists)
Stalemate: no legal move and NOT in check = draw
Castling (moving the king to safety while activating a rook, in a single move) and the special pawn capture en passant — the last two rules a beginner needs to play a full, legal game

Spotting undefended (hanging) pieces — yours and the opponent's

Deciding if a capture is safe by counting attackers vs defenders
Attacking two targets at once (gateway to the fork)

K+Q vs K technique part 1: pushing the lone king to the edge

Checkmating with two rooks using the rolling/ladder method

The knight fork (a double attack delivered by the knight)
Forks made by the queen, rook, bishop, and pawn (the whole fork family, including the royal fork)

The skewer — the pin's twin, attacking the more valuable piece first

stages.name: Knight
stages.theme: Tactical Vision — the full tactical toolkit + first endgames + opening principles
primary_concepts: Deepening knight forks in more complex positions
Forks by every piece; choosing the right target
Pins to the king (absolute) vs to a piece (relative)
Winning a pinned piece by attacking it again
Skewer technique and distinguishing pin vs skewer
Applying forks, pins, and skewers in guided games
Review of forks, pins, and skewers
The discovered attack — unveiling a rear piece's attack by moving the front piece
The discovered check — unveiling a check from the rear piece by moving the front piece
The double check — moving a piece so it gives check while also uncovering a check from the piece behind it, so two pieces check at once
Combining two tactics into one combination — a forcing first move (most often a check that also threatens material) that the opponent must answer, followed by a second tactic that wins

Removing the defender — capturing or chasing away the piece that guards a key target so the target can be won, knowing that a defended target falls cleanly only when it is frozen by a pin or when the guard is removed WITH check
Applying the Unit 2 tactics — discovered attacks and checks, double checks, two-tactic combinations, and removing the defender — in guided games
Review of Unit 2 — discovered attacks and checks, double checks, two-tactic combinations, and removing the defender
The back-rank mate — a king trapped behind its own unmoved pawns is mated by a rook or queen reaching the open back rank with check — together with its defence, making luft

Scholar's Mate — aiming the queen and a bishop at f7 (the square only the king defends) so two attackers beat one defender — together with its defence: developing with tempo, counting attackers versus defenders, and punishing the early queen

Smothered mate — a knight delivering checkmate to a king whose escape squares are all blocked by its own pieces, including the queen-sacrifice setup that forces the enemy to self-block the final flight square

Anastasia's mate and the Arabian mate — two knight-and-rook patterns in which the knight removes the king's escape squares and guards the rook, so the rook can mate a king on the edge or in the corner
Forced mate in two — selecting a forcing first move and then proving checkmate against every possible reply, the foundation of accurate attacking calculation
Rapid recognition of the Unit 3 mating patterns — back-rank, Scholar's, smothered, Anastasia's, Arabian, and the forced mate-in-two — and delivering the mate under time pressure
Review of Unit 3 — the named checkmate patterns (back-rank, Scholar's, smothered, Anastasia's, Arabian) and the forced mate-in-two
Assessment of Level 2A tactics and mating patterns on novel positions
Deflection — forcing an enemy piece to leave a square or duty it is required to hold, then exploiting the abandoned square.
Decoy and attraction — luring an enemy piece (usually the king) onto a fatal square with a forcing check or sacrifice, then striking with a fork or mate.
Removing the defender — eliminating the enemy piece that guards a key target square or mating square, then capturing the undefended target or delivering mate.
Overloading — exploiting an enemy piece burdened with two or more defensive duties by attacking one duty with a forcing move so the other target collapses.

The in-between move (zwischenzug) — inserting a forcing move, usually a check or a larger threat, BEFORE the expected reply or recapture, so the opponent is forced into a worse outcome; and interference — interposing a piece to cut the line between an enemy piece and what it guards.

Tactical pattern recognition: identifying WHICH advanced-tactic motif is present (deflection, decoy, removing the defender, overloading, or the in-between move) before calculating, then executing the combination the motif points to.

Review of Unit 4 — the advanced-tactic motifs (deflection, decoy & attraction, removing the defender, overloading, interference / in-between move) and IDENTIFYING which one a mixed position calls for before solving.

Checkmating a lone king with king and rook (the box method): the rook cuts the enemy king into a box, your king comes up to take the opposition, you shrink the box step by step with rook checks, and the rook mates on the edge — never stalemating.

The opposition in king-and-pawn-versus-king endings: kings face each other with one empty square between, and the side not to move forces the other king aside. The attacker uses it to escort the king in front of the pawn to a key square and queen (king first, not pawn first); the defender uses it to block and draw; the rook-pawn corner is the drawn exception.

Two tools for deciding whether a lone king can catch a passed pawn: the rule of the square (for an unescorted pawn, draw the square whose side is the pawn's moves to promote — counting a 2nd-rank pawn from the 3rd — and the king catches it if inside the square or able to step in on its move) and key squares (when your own king escorts, lead it onto a square two ranks ahead of the pawn to queen by force).

Passed pawns decide endings: a passed pawn has no enemy pawn ahead of it or on the adjacent files, so only a king can stop it. Today's job is to RECOGNISE one and to CREATE one — by a pawn breakthrough that sacrifices to clear a lane, or by capturing away from the enemy king to make an outside passer. (The protected passer is named as a preview, and pushing the passer home is revision of S072-S073.)

A promotion race is decided by counting tempi: count how many single steps each passed pawn needs to reach the back rank — the side to move effectively counts one fewer, and queening even one move earlier wins. When the enemy can also queen, promote WITH TEMPO: a new queen that gives CHECK skewers the enemy king and the enemy queen when they share a file, rank, or diagonal, and wins the queen. If an enemy pawn blocks your runner, sacrifice a pawn to deflect it, then count the survivor home.

Endgame technique under resistance: NAME the fundamental endgame type (king-and-rook mate, the opposition, the square of the pawn, passed pawns, promotion races), state the winning or drawing plan, then execute it against an opponent who defends actively — converting basic wins and holding basic draws.

Interleaved review of the unit's five fundamental endgames: NAME the type cold (king-and-rook mate, the opposition, the square of the pawn, passed pawns, promotion races), decide whether to convert / hold / evaluate, then execute the plan that type calls for — with no theme announced to give the answer away.

The center is the four squares d4, e4, d5 and e5 — the high ground of the board. A piece in the center reaches the most squares and can swing to either wing fastest, so the first job of the opening is to fight for these squares. There are three ways to fight: OCCUPY the center with a pawn (1.e4 or 1.d4 grabs space and controls the squares beside it), DEVELOP knights and bishops so they attack central squares, and CHALLENGE an enemy pawn that lands in the center by striking it with a pawn of your own. When you must recapture, take TOWARD the center to keep a pawn in the middle.

Development means getting your pieces off the back rank and into the game. In the opening you have four minor pieces — two knights and two bishops — asleep at home, and the player who wakes them up fastest, on the best squares, gets the attack first. Three rules guide development: (1) Knights before bishops — a knight belongs on f3/c3 (or ...f6/...c6) where it hits the center, and that square is clear from move one, while a bishop should wait until you can see which diagonal is best. (2) Bring out a NEW piece every move — never shuffle the same piece twice or drag the queen out early to be chased. (3) Develop toward the center and castle — each piece should fight for the middle and clear the path so the king can castle to safety. A lead in development means more pieces ready to attack.

King safety is the first job of the opening. While your king sits in the center on e1 (or e8), it is exposed: the moment the central files and diagonals open, enemy pieces deliver checks and the king has nowhere to hide. Castling solves this in a single move — the king jumps two squares toward a corner and a rook leaps to its other side, so the king ends up tucked behind an unbroken wall of three pawns while a rook swings toward the center. The rule of thumb is to castle EARLY, usually by about move ten, as soon as you have developed a knight and a bishop and cleared the squares between king and rook. You can castle king-side (the short castle, O-O) behind the f-, g- and h-pawns, or queen-side (the long castle, O-O-O) behind the a-, b- and c-pawns; choose the side whose pawn shield is still intact. If a piece still blocks the path, first develop that last piece — then castle next move. Develop, get the king safe, THEN attack.

Good opening play has three simple rules — take the center, develop your pieces, and castle your king to safety. "Opening Don'ts" are the three classic ways beginners break those rules, and each one hands the opponent free time. DON'T bring your queen out too early: the queen is your most valuable piece, so the moment it stands in the open the enemy develops knights and bishops that attack it, and you waste move after move running it to safety while your opponent brings out a whole army. DON'T move the same piece twice in the opening without a real reason: every move you re-touch one developed piece is a move you did NOT use to wake up a sleeping one, so you fall behind in development. DON'T grab pawns with pieces in the opening: chasing a stray pawn drags a piece offside, costs tempo, and often leaves your king stuck in the center while the opponent opens lines. The flip side is just as important: when your OPPONENT breaks a Don't, punish it — develop a piece that attacks the early queen, so you gain time for free, then finish developing and castle. Develop with purpose, one new piece at a time, and let greedy or careless opponents lose the race.

The Opera Game is the most famous teaching game in chess history: in 1858 the American champion Paul Morphy, playing White against two amateurs (the Duke of Brunswick and Count Isouard) during a night at the opera, won in just seventeen moves by doing nothing magical — only following the opening principles you have already learned, one after another, perfectly. He took the center with 1.e4 and 3.d4. He developed a new piece almost every move — Nf3, Bc4, Nc3, Bg5 — always toward the center and always with a purpose, often hitting something so that he gained time. He castled (12.O-O-O) and in the very same move swung his rook onto the open d-file, straight at Black's uncastled king. His opponents, meanwhile, broke the rules: they left pieces at home, wasted moves, and never got their king to safety. Once every White piece was working and every Black piece was tangled up, Morphy finished with a combination — the breakthrough 13.Rxd7 to remove a defender, and the dazzling queen sacrifice 16.Qb8+!! that decoys the last guard so that 17.Rd8# is checkmate. The lesson of the Opera Game is simple and powerful: you do not need tricks to win in the opening — develop every piece, castle your king, aim at the enemy king, and the tactics will appear by themselves. Lead in development is the engine; the sacrifice is just the finish.

Interleaved review of the unit's opening principles: NAME the principle at work (control the center, develop, castle early) or SPOT the opening Don't being broken (early queen, moving a piece twice, grabbing pawns), then play the principled move — with no theme announced to give the answer away.

Comprehensive interleaved review of the whole of Stage 2 across THREE domains: NAME the kind of position cold (a tactic to calculate, an endgame to convert or hold, or an opening to develop), PICK the right tool, then solve — with no theme announced to give the answer away.

Final Knight Stage assessment on NOVEL positions across THREE domains: NAME the kind of position cold (a tactic to calculate, an endgame to convert, or an opening to develop), PICK the right tool, and solve — with no theme announced. Passing graduates the student to the Bishop Stage.

stages.name: Bishop
stages.theme: The Thinking Player — evaluation, pawn structure, planning, rook endgames
primary_concepts: The four questions of evaluation — material, king safety, activity, pawn structure — combined into a single verdict
Material imbalances: judging positions where the two sides hold different pieces of similar value, and who the imbalance favours.
Piece activity as an evaluation factor
King safety as an evaluation factor
Full evaluation: a two-factor verdict followed by a quiet press
A quick four-question scan (material, king safety, activity, pawn structure) tells you who is better and which factor is decisive — and the decisive factor points straight to the move.

THE PLAN in evaluation: a quick four-question scan (material, king safety, activity, pawn structure) tells you who is better and which factor is decisive — and the decisive factor points straight to the move. In this Unit-1 review the positions are deliberately interleaved so that no two consecutive puzzles turn on the same factor: students must re-run the scan on every board and ask "who is better here, and why?" instead of repeating the previous answer.
The dual nature of the isolated central pawn
The dual nature of doubled pawns
Backward pawns and the holes in front of them
Passed pawns and protected passed pawns — what they are, why a protected passer is the strongest pawn on the board because the enemy king is chained to it, and the two ways to create one.
Pawn chains and the breaks that challenge them
A pawn-structure feature on the board tells you the plan, and naming the feature first makes the right move easy to find.

THE PLAN in pawn-structure play: the structure on the board tells you the plan. An isolated or backward pawn is a fixed target — blockade the square in front of it, then attack it; doubled pawns are a weakness to blockade AND a half-open file for the other side to seize; a passed pawn wants to be guarded by another pawn, because a protected passer needs no piece to babysit it; a pawn chain is broken at its base. In this Unit-2 review the positions are interleaved so that no two consecutive puzzles share the same feature, and almost every answer is a QUIET move — students must re-read every board and ask "what is the structure here, and what plan does it demand?" instead of hunting for a tactic or repeating the previous answer.
Placing rooks on open and half-open files
The power of a rook (or pair) on the 7th rank
Establishing knights on protected, unattackable outpost squares
Bishop quality relative to one's own pawn chains
The bishop pair as an activity weapon in open play
THE PLAN: in any position, scan all your pieces, find the worst-placed one, and make the move that gives it the best job right now.

THE PLAN in piece placement: every piece has a dream square, and the position tells you which piece to improve and where. In this Unit-3 review the positions are deliberately interleaved so that no two consecutive puzzles turn on the same placement tool: students must ask "which piece wants a better square here, and where?" on every board — a rook craving an open file or the 7th rank, a knight hunting an outpost, a good bishop wanting an open diagonal, or the bishop pair looking to rake the board — instead of repeating the previous answer.
Assessment of Level 3A evaluation, pawn structure, and piece placement on novel positions
What a plan is — naming the enemy's weakest target, choosing a method to attack it, and playing the purposeful move that carries the method out
Systematically improving your least active piece

Prophylaxis (from the Greek for 'to guard beforehand') is the habit of asking 'What does my opponent want to do?' before deciding your own move. Strong players do not chase their own ideas in a vacuum — they constantly read the other side's intentions and play moves that neutralise those intentions, ideally before the threat is even fully formed. Prophylaxis is not passive defence; it is efficient play. A single well-timed preventive move costs almost no time yet eliminates an entire plan of counterplay, freeing you to pursue your own goals without interruption. There are three tools of prevention, and the position tells you which to reach for: (1) REMOVE THE ATTACKER — capture or drive away the piece that creates the threat, killing it at the source; (2) REPOSITION or OVER-GUARD — move the threatened piece out of reach, or add a defender / cover the key square so the threat no longer bites; and (3) the IN-BETWEEN counter — when your own resources are faster, answer a threat with an even bigger threat instead of meekly defending. In every position today the opponent has just made a threatening move, and your job is to find the one reply that stops their idea cold — a reply that, checked by the engine, is also the objectively best move on the board.
Creating and using weaknesses — spotting an enemy target that cannot defend itself and pressing it, switching to a second when the first is held

One of the most important — and most often neglected — skills in chess is knowing what to do once you are already winning. The answer, taught by the great champions since Jose Raul Capablanca in the early twentieth century, is deceptively simple: when you are ahead in material, trade pieces and simplify. Every even exchange of pieces removes one of the opponent's resources. Their bishops, knights, and rooks are the tools they need to create counterplay, complicate the position, and confuse you. Each time you swap one off the board, their chances shrink and your extra material becomes relatively more powerful — because there are fewer pieces left to fight your advantage. Crucially, you must trade pieces but keep your pawns: pawns are your endgame currency. In a simplified position, an extra pawn marches down the board and queens; an extra piece with nothing to do in a crowded position can feel invisible. When the opponent's king is stuck in the centre on top of everything else, the resulting endgame after simplification is almost always an easy technical win — the king becomes a liability rather than an asset. This is called conversion technique, and it is a mark of the truly strategic player.

THE PLAN is the master skill that ties every other strategic tool together. A strong player does not drift from move to move hoping something good happens; they pause, survey the whole board, and choose a specific goal. But choosing a goal is only step one — the real discipline is stating it in a single, honest sentence before touching a piece, then following through on it even when the opponent makes it inconvenient. In this session, THE PLAN functions as an umbrella: underneath it live all four tools students have studied in Unit 4. At any given moment the position will call for one (or sometimes two) of those tools, and the planner's job is to read the position correctly — Is my worst piece a rook stuck on a closed file? Then improve it. Is my opponent about to activate a dangerous piece? Then stop it first. Am I holding one weakness but the opponent is defending it easily? Then open a second front. Am I up material with the queens off? Then trade pieces and march pawns. Stating the plan aloud — to a partner, a coach, or even to themselves — builds the metacognitive habit that separates strategic players from reactive ones. Adjusting the plan is not a failure; it is proof that the student is reading the new position honestly rather than clinging to a plan the board has already refuted.

THE PLAN in the middlegame and the endgame: the position on the board tells you which planning tool to reach for. Your own passive piece is a candidate to ACTIVATE onto its best square; a hole or a straggler is a TARGET to name and occupy; the opponent's idea is something to PREVENT before you push your own; a weakness that cannot be defended by a pawn is one half of the two-weakness plan; and a position you are already winning asks for CONVERSION technique instead of a fresh attack. In this Unit-4 review the positions are deliberately interleaved so that no two consecutive puzzles share the same tool — students must re-read every board and ask "what does THIS position need?" instead of repeating the previous answer. The middlegame boards are White to move and the conversion boards are Black to move, so colour changes with every puzzle too.
forced three-move combination
the Greek Gift sacrifice (Bxh7+)
sacrificing material for a decisive attack

The saving capture (liquidation into insufficient material): capturing the opponent's last dangerous piece so that neither side has enough material to force checkmate, turning a lost game into an immediate draw.

Forced perpetual check: a returning loop of two consecutive checks where each forces the king's only legal reply, returning the position to its start; doubling the loop produces threefold repetition and an automatic draw.

The Immortal Game is the most famous attacking game ever played. In 1851, during a break in a London tournament, Adolf Anderssen (White) beat Lionel Kieseritzky in a friendly game so dazzling that it was nicknamed 'immortal'. Anderssen opened with the King's Gambit (1.e4 e5 2.f4), offering a pawn to rip open the centre and aim at Black's king. Black grabbed the pawn and then went hunting with the queen (3...Qh4+), winning a little material but developing almost nothing. While Black chased pawns and shuffled the same queen and knight around, Anderssen poured pieces into the game and built a battery on the g-file. When everything was aimed at the enemy king, the fireworks began. Anderssen did not count material — he counted DEFENDERS. He let a bishop go, then played 18.Bd6!!, a quiet-looking move that offers BOTH rooks just to block the black bishop's retreat and choke the king's escape squares. Black took both rooks and even checked with the queen, but it did not matter: 21.Nxg7+ dragged the king out, and 22.Qf6+!! gave up the queen to decoy the last defender, so that 23.Be7# was checkmate — delivered by three minor pieces while Black had a queen, a rook, and a bishop sitting uselessly on the other side of the board. The lesson is the biggest idea in attacking chess: material does not defend a king — pieces do. If you are far ahead in development and every piece is aimed at the enemy king, look for the forcing move that removes the last defender, and be willing to give up material to land it.

Win-or-Save recognition: the first diagnostic question in any mixed position is 'Am I attacking for mate or defending for a draw?' — this master switch routes you to the correct Unit 5 toolkit without wasted effort.
Winning the Lucena position by 'building a bridge' — putting the rook on the fourth rank so it can interpose against the defender's side checks, freeing the king to shepherd the pawn to promotion

Drawing the Philidor position by the third-rank defense — keeping the king in front of the pawn and the rook on the third rank in front of it, then switching to long-range checks from behind once the pawn reaches the sixth rank
Activating the rook in a rook endgame — the Tarrasch rule (rook behind the passed pawn) and cutting the enemy king off — so a passed pawn, escorted by the king, promotes safely

An opening repertoire is the set of openings you play regularly — your personal toolkit. A good repertoire is built on IDEAS, not memorized move sequences. Every opening has a core purpose, and once you know it, you can find good moves even in positions you have never seen. The four building-block ideas are: (1) CENTER BREAK — strike the center with a pawn to d4, d5, e4, or e5, claiming space and opening lines; (2) FLANK CHALLENGE — push a pawn to c4, c5, f4, or f5 to attack the enemy's center from the side, undermining their d- or e-pawn; (3) DEVELOPING PRESSURE — bring a knight or bishop off the back rank to a square that attacks an enemy piece, putting the opponent under immediate tactical stress; (4) CENTER SUPPORT — advance a pawn so it defends a friendly pawn already in the center zone, keeping your central pawn structure solid. When you choose an opening, ask: 'What is this opening TRYING TO DO?' If the answer is clear — 'the Italian breaks with d4', 'the Colle supports d4 with c3', 'the Sicilian challenges with c5' — then you have a plan for every move, even when the game leaves the book line. A repertoire built on ideas survives deviations; a repertoire built on memorization collapses the moment the opponent plays something different.

Practice transforms knowledge into habit. In S125, you learned the four building-block ideas behind every opening plan — center break, flank challenge, developing pressure, and center support. In this practice session, you revisit each idea on the same openings so that recognition becomes automatic. The goal is not to learn something new; it is to make what you already know faster, more confident, and more reliable under game conditions. Spaced repetition — revisiting an idea after a short gap — is one of the most powerful learning techniques in cognitive science. Each time you encounter the same idea in the same opening, the neural pathway gets stronger and retrieval gets quicker. By the end of this session, naming the core idea of the Italian, Caro-Kann, Colle, Pirc, London, and QGD should feel like naming the color of a piece — instant and effortless.

THE PLAN in the rook endgame: the position tells you which technique to reach for. An enemy king on the queening file is a target to CUT OFF with a check; your own passed pawn wants the ROOK BEHIND it; a king stuck in front of its pawn must MARCH out to the shelter side; incoming checks are stopped by BUILDING THE BRIDGE; a pawn on the last rank is there to PROMOTE; and a lone enemy king on the edge is finished with the KING-AND-ROOK MATE. In this Unit-6 review the positions are interleaved so no two consecutive puzzles share the same technique — students must re-read every board and ask "which step of the rook-endgame method does THIS position need?" instead of repeating the previous answer.

THE PLAN across the whole Bishop Stage: EVALUATE the position, NAME the Stage-3 idea it turns on, STATE the plan, then PLAY the move. In this comprehensive review the positions are deliberately interleaved so that no two consecutive puzzles share a theme: students must ask "what does THIS position turn on — an evaluation factor, a structural weakness, a piece-placement tool, a plan, or an endgame technique?" on every board instead of repeating the previous answer.
Whole-stage assessment of the six Bishop-Stage skills on novel positions; graduation to the Rook Stage

stages.name: Rook
stages.theme: The Complete Player — attack/defense, calculation, advanced strategy & endgames, tournament skills
primary_concepts: Attacking the castled king with open lines and more attackers

Pawns are not just defenders or future queens-in-waiting — they are immediate attackers. A well-timed pawn advance or capture can shatter the enemy king's shelter, tear open files for heavy pieces, or become an unstoppable promotion threat that decides the game on its own.
Line-opening sacrifices — giving up material to open a file, rank, or diagonal for a heavy piece to deliver checkmate through the opened line.
The exchange sacrifice — giving a rook for a minor piece for activity or attack

Defence is a skill, not a surrender. When the opponent attacks, calm players do not freeze or grab material blindly — they read the attack, find its spearhead, and choose the resource that meets it. This session builds a defender's toolbox and a habit for using it: the ASSESS-CHOOSE-CALCULATE loop. ASSESS the threat and name the piece delivering it; CHOOSE the resource that fits; CALCULATE the line to a safe result. There are three resources you will use directly today, and two more for your games: (1) TRADE or REMOVE THE ATTACKER — capture or exchange off the piece making the threat, killing it at the source; (2) RELOCATE and DEFEND — regroup a piece to guard the key square, over-guard it, or hem in and trap an over-extended invader; (3) COUNTERATTACK — when your own blow lands first, answer a threat with a bigger one, an in-between check or capture that seizes the initiative; (4) RETURN MATERIAL — when ahead, give some back to break the attack and simplify into a safe, winning position; and (5) the FORTRESS — a wall of pawns and pieces the enemy cannot breach, used to hold a draw from a worse position. Calculation matters most in defence, because a single overlooked check can undo everything. In every position today the opponent has just attacked, and your task is to pick the resource that meets it and calculate it out — a move that, checked by the engine, is also the objectively best move on the board.
Sparring with both attack and defence: switch roles at the board, calculate the right method, and execute it with confidence.

A fighting game has two modes, and reading which one you are in comes first: attack when the enemy king is the weaker, defend when yours is — then run THE CALCULATE to prove the plan. Attack by naming a target, opening lines with a storm or sacrifice, and calculating a forced mate; defend by assessing the threat, choosing an active resource, and calculating that your king ends up safe.
Strong players do not play the first move that jumps out at them. They generate a short list of candidate moves and calculate each one to the end, then play the move they have proven is best.

Calculating a forced line: stringing together checks, captures, and threats so that every opponent reply is forced, and following the sequence accurately to its conclusion — here, a three-move forced checkmate.

Visualization is the mental skill of holding a future position clearly in your mind's eye — seeing exactly where each piece will stand after a forced sequence — so you can judge the outcome before you ever move a piece.

A critical moment is the instant a game hangs in the balance — a forcing tactic is on the board and one routine, autopilot move can throw the whole game away — so the skill is a two-part habit: first RECOGNISE the moment from its trigger signs, then SLOW DOWN and CALCULATE the forcing line to its end before you play.

The blunder-check is a habit you run before every move: once you have a candidate, you assume the opponent will answer with their STRONGEST reply — not the weak or hoped-for one — and you calculate your move to the end against that best defence; only if it still wins or mates do you play it, because most blunders come from calculating only the opponent's obvious answer.
Calculation is a trainable habit: pick a forcing candidate, assume the opponent's best reply, calculate the whole line to checkmate in your head, verify it, then play.

Strong calculation is recognition plus proof: name the mating pattern you are steering toward, then run THE CALCULATE — candidate, assume the best reply, calculate the whole line to checkmate in your head, verify, and play.
isolated queen's pawn
hanging pawns
minority attack
space advantage
open position

A pawn structure has a name, and the name comes with a plan already attached. Recognising the structure hands you the plan, the plan hands you two or three candidate moves, and THE CALCULATE tells you which one to play — so naming the structure is the fastest way to stop drifting in a middlegame.
Strong strategic play begins with recognition: the pawn structure tells you which plan belongs to the position, and THE CALCULATE then proves whether your chosen move actually delivers that plan.

Practical endgame play is a three-step decision: name the endgame family, state the goal (convert, hold, or mate), then calculate the committal move — trade, push, or promotion — to the very end before playing it.

Complex-endgame mastery is the review ritual made automatic: name the family (it loads the right toolkit), state the goal (convert, hold, or mate), then calculate the committal move to the very end before playing it.

The clock is a resource to budget just like material: sort every position into SNAP — play on rhythm in 10-20 seconds when it is a recapture, a known pattern, or a choice between equal safe moves — or INVEST — spend 2-5 minutes when there is a forcing sequence, a sacrifice, or an irreversible decision, and run THE CALCULATE to the very end before touching a piece — because time trouble means playing the most important moves of the game on seconds.

Full algebraic notation is the written language of chess — piece letter plus destination square, x for captures, + for check, # for mate, =Q for promotion, O-O and O-O-O for castling, and a from-file or from-rank like Rgxg8 or Q6xg7 when two identical pieces can reach the same square — kept on a scoresheet in the tournament order of play the move FIRST, then write it; and it lives alongside the laws of the tournament hall: touch-move with 'I adjust', the same-hand clock press, and the etiquette of silence, polite draw offers, handshakes, and raising a hand for the arbiter.

The four-step calming routine — BREATHE (one slow breath, drop the shoulders), LOOK (name the opponent's biggest threat out loud in your head), CALCULATE (run the candidate line to the very end exactly as THE CALCULATE taught, before the hand moves under touch-move), and TRUST (play the calculated line without flinching, even through a mid-line counter-check) — practised under a growth mindset that normalises nerves as universal (even world champions feel them), treats pressure as a signal to slow down rather than speed up, and treats every mistake as information for the next game rather than a verdict on the player.

A repeatable six-item pre-game preparation routine, the Round-Ready checklist, in which BODY covers sleep, food and water, BAG covers set, clock, scoresheet, pen and routine card packed the night before, BOARD covers arriving early and setting up correctly with a white square bottom-right and each queen on her own colour, BRAIN covers a short timed warm-up of quick forced mates to wake pattern recognition, BEARINGS covers the pairing sheet, colour, opponent and a first move chosen in advance for each colour, and BREATH covers one slow breath before move one, so that nothing at all is left to be decided in the five minutes when a player is least able to decide well.

Opening depth is not more memorised moves: it is knowing which question the position is asking. Where the book ends, the four opening jobs answer it; where the pawns are uneven, the count answers it; where you know your opponent, his habit answers it; where a piece has strayed, its escape squares answer it; and where a plan has already created a weakness, only a calculated line answers it.

Advanced endgame technique starts with a judgement, not a move: name the ending, decide whether the position is one to convert or one to hold, and only then choose the move — because the converting move and the holding move are frequently different moves on the same board.

An advanced endgame is solved in one fixed order — name the ending, count what each side needs, state the verdict, then choose the move that verdict demands — and the review proves why the order matters: the same trade wins one card, strips a king on another and draws a third, so only the verdict distinguishes them.

A study plan is honest when every slot is a measured weakness and the minutes follow the measurement: count your own priced mistakes, name each one, give the most minutes to the fault you make most often, and start the week with the fault that costs most each time.

The unit's five instruments are five different questions about the same move, and they do not agree: across the 70 free moves of one fresh game, S186 can name a fault on 8, S187 calls 3 critical, S188 has something to teach on 9, S189 permits a mark on 18 and S190 finds 51 crossroads — so the first move of any analysis is deciding which question you are asking.

Creative play is not one skill but two, and the first move of every creative decision is choosing between them: if a forced finish exists the position is countable and calculation settles it completely, and if none exists the position can only be judged — by counting compensation against a bar, or by weighing what a bold move gains against how many good continuations survive it.

Creative play is two instruments and one habit: if a forced finish exists the position is countable and only a proof will do, and if it does not then the resource can only be priced — so the first move of every creative decision is choosing the instrument, and this review proves the choice cannot be read off the difficulty, because every tier band contains both a countable card and a judgeable one.

A playing style is a preference exercised inside the board's limits, never a plan applied to every position: the board decides which instrument has jurisdiction and whether it says go or stop, and only when both roads sit inside the forty-centipawn band that makes two moves worth the same does the choice come back to the player — which is why this review can alternate attacking and positional answers card by card, put both inside every tier band, and answer five of its eight cards with a refusal.

Competition is chess with the world let back in: a standing, a body, a file, a record and an audience each get a vote that the position alone does not contain, and the discipline of Unit 6 is to name the voice, ask what it wants, and price it — which is why the same board can be a must-win and a safe board with two different right moves, why the only voice that asks you to give centipawns away on purpose asks for almost none of them, and why the review can put a 851-centipawn error on a Foundation card and a costless one on a Challenge card.
